title: Climbing Mount Rainier by the Disappointment Cleaver
description: Theodore Walrond's July 2020 guided climb of Mount Rainier with International Mountain Guides: Camp Muir, Ingraham Flats and a pre-dawn push up the Cleaver.
html:
Mount Rainier was the first mountain I ever stood on top of. In July 2020 I climbed it with International Mountain Guides by the Disappointment Cleaver route, the most traveled way up the mountain and still a serious glacier climb: about 18 miles round trip and roughly 9,000 feet of gain to a 14,411-foot summit.

How the climb was staged

Rainier is big enough to make its own weather, so the climb ran over several days instead of one long push. We started at Paradise and climbed to Camp Muir at 10,080 feet, the rocky high camp used by most parties on this side of the mountain. From there we moved up again to Ingraham Flats at about 11,400 feet, which takes a real chunk out of summit day.

Summit day

Summit day on the Cleaver starts in the dark. Rope teams leave before dawn so they can cross the Ingraham Glacier and climb the Cleaver while the snow is still firm, then come back down before the afternoon sun softens the slopes. Glacier travel means crevasse hazard, which is why every step above Camp Muir happened on a rope with a guide.

What I'd tell someone thinking about it

  • Go guided for a first glaciated peak. The guides handled route-finding, rope systems and the calls on weather and timing, which let me focus on moving well.
  • Train for long days, not one hard hour. The challenge is several days of carrying weight uphill at altitude and still having something left for an alpine start.
  • Trust the staging. Sleeping higher at Ingraham Flats made summit day shorter and safer.

Rainier is the traditional proving ground for bigger mountains, and it's the reason Denali is on my list. The rest of my trips, from the Four Pass Loop to the High Sierra, are in my field notes.

caption: On the snow on Mount Rainier, July 2020.

title: Teaching Scuba in Florida's Springs: Notes From UF Scientific Diving
seo_title: Teaching Scuba in Florida's Springs at UF
description: Theodore Walrond on three years as a divemaster and teaching assistant for UF's Scientific Diving Program, and the springs where he dives.
html:
From 2020 to 2023 I was a divemaster and teaching assistant for the University of Florida's Scientific Diving Program. I'm an SDI Divemaster, and that work meant helping more than 30 students move through courses from Open Water up to Master Diver.

What the job involved

Most of it happened in three places: in the water, running skills and keeping an eye on students; out of the water, helping with gear and checks; and in the classroom, supporting lectures on dive planning, dive physics and physiology. The classroom part matters more than people expect. Understanding why pressure, gas and depth behave the way they do is what makes the in-water skills stick.

Florida's springs

Almost all of my diving has been in Florida karst: freshwater springs and cavern systems that are cold, clear and, in places, overhead. It's its own discipline, nothing like reef diving, and cavern areas call for proper training and conservative planning. Sites in my log include Devil's Den and Blue Grotto in Williston, Ginnie Springs in High Springs, Troy Spring and Royal Spring along the Suwannee, Hudson Grotto, and my favorite, Paradise Spring near Ocala. The one saltwater outlier so far is the kelp forest off Catalina Island.

What teaching taught me

  • Calm is contagious. Students take their cue from whoever is leading, especially when something goes slightly wrong.
  • Simple instructions win. Underwater you can't explain much, so the briefing on land has to do the work.
  • Checks are a habit, not a step. The best divers I worked with never skipped them, no matter how routine the dive.

Next on the dive list: the Silfra fissure in Iceland, a manta ray night dive in Kona and the Great Blue Hole in Belize. The full log is in my field notes.
alt: Theodore Walrond diving in a Florida spring
caption: Diving one of Florida's freshwater springs.

title: Reading 300 Studies: How I Approach a Research Question
description: Theodore Walrond on what evidence reviews at UF's McKnight Brain Institute and Romark Laboratories taught him about organizing research before interpreting it.
html:
Two research projects shaped how I read evidence. At the University of Florida's McKnight Brain Institute, from 2022 to 2023, I worked through more than 300 studies on whether a subarachnoid hemorrhage can leave someone more vulnerable to Alzheimer's disease. Before that, in the summer of 2021, I tracked more than 25 COVID-19 drug candidates for Romark Laboratories in Tampa and reviewed over 400 articles on one older drug, niclosamide. Here's the approach I took away from both.

1. Pin down the question first

A broad topic produces an endless reading list. A specific question, such as whether one kind of brain injury predicts a later disease, tells you which papers matter and which can wait.

2. Organize before you interpret

At Romark the tool was a set of dashboards that logged every candidate by efficacy, trial phase and mechanism of action. Seeing those three things side by side made it obvious which drugs had both a plausible mechanism and maturing evidence. A clear structure surfaces patterns faster than reading alone.

3. Weigh studies by design, not by headline

An animal study, a small clinical series and a large patient follow-up can all point the same way and still deserve very different weight. Promising lab results and proven benefit in people are not the same thing.

4. Look for agreement, conflict and gaps

The most useful output of the McKnight review was not a single answer. It was a framework of the variables that seemed to connect vascular injury to neurodegeneration, such as inflammation, damage to the blood-brain barrier and slower clearance of waste from brain tissue, along with where the evidence was thin. Those gaps are what point to the next experiment.

5. Explain it to people outside your corner

Presenting the findings to faculty from three departments forced the framework to make sense to people who didn't share my reading list. If it can't survive that, it isn't finished.

I've since moved from research toward the business side of health, but this is still how I approach any hard question. A plain-language look at the brain-bleed question itself is on rexwalrond.com.

title: Bowman Lake to Kintla Lake: Backpacking Glacier's Quiet Corner
seo_title: Backpacking Glacier: Bowman to Kintla Lake
description: Theodore Walrond's August 2023 trip across the northwest corner of Glacier National Park, from Bowman Lake over Brown Pass and Boulder Pass to Kintla Lake.
html:
In August 2023 I backpacked from Bowman Lake to Kintla Lake in the far northwest corner of Glacier National Park: about 32 miles over Brown Pass and Boulder Pass, in the part of the park where the crowds thin to almost nobody.

The route

The trail leaves Bowman Lake and climbs to Brown Pass, then carries on over Boulder Pass, the high point at roughly 7,470 feet, before dropping down the far side to Kintla Lake. Published figures put the total gain around 5,500 feet. Those are route numbers rather than GPS tracks, but they're close enough to plan against.

What to expect

  • Grizzly country the whole way. Food storage and bear awareness are part of every hour on this trail, not an afterthought.
  • Remote terrain. There are few easy ways out once you're committed, so conditions and planning matter more than usual.
  • Limited permits. The backcountry campsite system does most of the work of keeping the route quiet.

Who it's for

If you want Glacier's lakes and passes without the traffic around the park's main roads, this is the route. It's also the trip on my list where the backcountry felt most remote. The rest of the list, from Colorado's Four Pass Loop to the High Sierra, is in my field notes.
alt: Theodore Walrond with a backpack at Bowman Lake in Glacier National Park
caption: Starting out at Bowman Lake, Glacier National Park, August 2023.

title: The Four Pass Loop: The Trip That Started It All
seo_title: The Four Pass Loop, Maroon Bells (2019)
description: Theodore Walrond's August 2019 trip around Colorado's Four Pass Loop: about 26 miles and four passes over 12,000 feet in the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness.
html:
Every list of trips starts somewhere. Mine starts with the Four Pass Loop, a circuit of about 26 miles through the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness outside Aspen, Colorado, which I backpacked in August 2019.

The route

The loop crosses four passes, every one of them above 12,000 feet: West Maroon, Frigid Air, Trail Rider and Buckskin. Each pass drops into a different drainage and then climbs straight back out of it, so the gain adds up fast. Published figures put it near 7,900 feet of climbing with a high point around 12,500 feet.

What makes it hard

Summer afternoons in the Elk Range bring a real chance of thunderstorms above treeline, and four high passes mean four exposed stretches to time. The rhythm that works is simple: start early, get over a pass before the clouds build, and camp lower in the next valley. The area is also a permit zone, so the planning starts long before the trailhead.

Why it mattered

It was the trip that made me want more. A year later I was on Mount Rainier, and since then I've added the John Muir Trail, the Teton Crest Trail, Glacier National Park and the High Sierra. Distances and conditions for each are in my field notes.

caption: On the Four Pass Loop, Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness, August 2019.

title: Seven Mountains: Notes From My Ski Log
seo_title: Ski Log: Alta, Snowbird, Telluride and More
description: Short notes from Theodore Walrond on the seven mountains he has skied in Utah, Colorado and Idaho, from Alta and Snowbird to Telluride and Sun Valley.
html:
Skiing is the one sport on my list that happens in winter, and so far it has taken me to seven mountains in three states. Four of them are in Utah, which says something about where the snow is.

Utah

  • Alta. At the top of Little Cottonwood Canyon, still skiers-only, and known for how much snow it collects.
  • Snowbird. Alta's neighbor in the same canyon, steeper and rockier, with an aerial tram that runs straight to the summit.
  • Deer Valley. Also skiers-only, with careful grooming and a capped daily crowd.
  • Park City. One of the largest ski areas in the country, which mostly means you won't run out of terrain in a day.

Colorado

  • Vail. Groomed runs on the front side and the wide-open Back Bowls behind.
  • Telluride. Steep terrain in the San Juan Mountains, with a free gondola linking the old mining town to Mountain Village.

Idaho

  • Sun Valley. America's first destination ski resort. Bald Mountain is one long, steady pitch from top to bottom.

When the snow melts I'm usually backpacking or diving instead. The full list of trips is in my field notes.
alt: Theodore Walrond skiing in Telluride, Colorado
caption: Skiing in Telluride, Colorado.

title: The Evolving Frontier of Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Research
description: What a subarachnoid hemorrhage is, why it's an emergency, and how research on diagnosing and treating these brain bleeds is moving forward, by Theodore Walrond.
html:
Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is a medical emergency caused by bleeding into the space surrounding the brain. This condition is not only lethal but also strikes suddenly, often without warning, primarily affecting individuals at the peak of their lives. Given its severity and the critical need for rapid intervention, SAH research is a dynamic and urgently evolving field. This article examines the strides being made in understanding, diagnosing, and treating SAH, highlighting the life-saving potential of ongoing research in this critical area of medicine.

Understanding Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

Subarachnoid hemorrhage typically results from the rupture of an aneurysm in one of the brain's arteries, leading to blood leaking into the subarachnoid space. This event causes sudden, severe headaches, often described by patients as "the worst headache of my life." Other symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness, and, in severe cases, loss of consciousness or even death.

The Importance of SAH Research

The urgency of advancing research in SAH cannot be overstated. Approximately 50% of SAH cases result in death, and many survivors face significant neurological impairments. Research aims not only to reduce mortality rates but also to improve the quality of life for survivors. This includes advancing emergency response techniques, refining surgical methods, and developing better post-operative care and rehabilitation practices.

Innovations in Diagnostic Technology

Early diagnosis is crucial in managing SAH effectively. Recent research has focused on enhancing imaging technologies such as CT scans and MRIs, which are vital for quick and accurate detection of cerebral aneurysms. Innovations like high-definition imaging and 3D reconstruction techniques have significantly improved clinicians' ability to assess the severity and specific characteristics of the bleed, allowing for more tailored and effective interventions.

Treatment Advancements

Treatment strategies for SAH have seen substantial improvements over the past decades. The mainstay of treatment involves securing the ruptured aneurysm to prevent rebleeding, which can be achieved through surgical clipping or endovascular coiling. Recent research has introduced novel biomaterials and endovascular devices that promise more effective and less invasive treatment options. Furthermore, there is an increasing focus on managing the complications of SAH, such as delayed cerebral ischemia, through new pharmacological agents that protect neural tissue and improve blood flow to the brain.

Genetic and Molecular Research

A growing area of SAH research involves understanding the genetic and molecular foundations of cerebral aneurysms. Identifying genetic markers and pathways that predispose individuals to SAH can lead to earlier identification of at-risk patients and potentially guide preventative treatments. Additionally, molecular studies are exploring the processes that weaken arterial walls, which could lead to innovative approaches to strengthen vascular structures before they become problematic.

Post-SAH Recovery and Rehabilitation

Surviving SAH is only the first step in what can be a long recovery journey. Research in neurorehabilitation has become increasingly important, focusing on restoring function and improving the quality of life for SAH survivors.

Overcoming Challenges in SAH Research

Conducting effective SAH research comes with numerous challenges. The sudden onset of the condition makes preemptive studies difficult, and the variability in how patients respond to treatments complicates clinical trials. Moreover, the need for multidisciplinary collaboration—from neurosurgeons and radiologists to rehabilitation specialists—requires coordinated efforts that are often hard to manage in fast-paced clinical settings. Overcoming these challenges requires not only innovative research designs but also substantial funding and institutional support.

The Future of SAH Research

The goal is to integrate genetic, molecular, and clinical data to tailor treatments to individual patients, enhancing the precision and effectiveness of interventions. Additionally, ongoing advancements in technology, such as artificial intelligence and machine learning, hold the promise of revolutionizing diagnostic and treatment paradigms, potentially predicting aneurysm risks and optimal treatment routes based on vast datasets.

A Call to Action

Subarachnoid hemorrhage remains a formidable challenge in the medical field, but the strides made through dedicated research offer hope. Each discovery not only brings us closer to understanding this complex condition but also to saving and improving the lives of those affected.

title: The Teton Crest Trail, With a Loop Over Paintbrush Divide
seo_title: Teton Crest Trail: Death Canyon to Paintbrush
description: Theodore Walrond's August 2022 extended loop on the Teton Crest Trail: about 50 miles via Death Canyon Shelf, Alaska Basin and Paintbrush Divide.
html:
The Teton Crest Trail runs along the west side of Wyoming's Teton Range, and in August 2022 I hiked an extended version of it: about 50 miles and 9,000 feet of gain, closing the loop over Paintbrush Divide instead of walking out the standard finish.

The route

The highlights come one after another: the long, exposed traverse of Death Canyon Shelf, the open meadows of Alaska Basin, and finally Paintbrush Divide, the high point at about 10,720 feet. The Grand, Middle and South Teton stay in view for most of the trip, which is the whole argument for doing this route.

Conditions

  • Exposure. Death Canyon Shelf is a high bench with big drops, beautiful and best done in good weather.
  • Snow on the divide. Even in August, snow can linger near Paintbrush Divide, so it pays to check conditions before committing.
  • Bear canister required. Grand Teton National Park requires approved food storage in the backcountry.

Of all the trips on my list, this is the one I'd recommend for the views per mile. Notes on the others, from the Four Pass Loop to Glacier and the High Sierra, are in my field notes.

caption: On the Teton Crest Trail, August 2022.
